analysis.one_liner: Makes expiring individual and small-business tax cuts permanent, including lower rates and the $2,000 child tax credit.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the two-year Congress ended, despite 104 Republican sponsors and cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 tax law cut individual income tax rates, roughly doubled the standard deduction, set a $2,000-per-child credit, gave pass-through business owners a 20% deduction, and doubled the estate tax exemption — but wrote most of those individual provisions to expire after 2025. This bill would erase that expiration and make all of it permanent. Nearly every taxpaying household would keep a real tax cut, but the largest and most expensive pieces — the doubled estate exemption, the 37% top rate, and the pass-through deduction — flow overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households, and the bill includes no offsets, so the whole cost lands on the deficit.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, virtually every household paying federal income tax would keep the lower rates and larger standard deduction instead of facing the tax increase scheduled when those provisions lapse. Families would keep the $2,000-per-child credit. Owners of partnerships, S corporations, and other pass-through businesses would keep a deduction worth 20% of their business income. Heirs of the largest estates would keep an estate tax exemption roughly double its pre-2017 size, and very high earners would keep the enlarged alternative minimum tax exemption.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpaying households, business owners, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Makes the reduced individual income tax rates — including the 37% top rate — permanent instead of letting them revert to higher pre-2017 rates after 2025.
Makes the larger standard deduction permanent; the bill sets it at $12,000 for single filers and $18,000 for joint filers in 2017 dollars, adjusted for inflation.
Makes the $2,000 child tax credit permanent, with up to $1,400 of it refundable for families who owe less in income tax than the credit is worth.
Makes permanent the deduction for qualified business income of pass-through entities such as partnerships and S corporations.
Doubles the estate and gift tax exemption amount, from a $5 million base to $10 million per person, indexed for inflation — a change that only matters for the largest estates.
Reinstates, after 2024, the rule that student loan debt forgiven because of a borrower's death or total permanent disability is not counted as taxable income — including for private student loans.
Expands allowable contributions to ABLE accounts for people with disabilities and lets 529 education savings funds roll over into them.
Expands what 529 education savings accounts can pay for, adding elementary and secondary school tuition, homeschool expenses, tutoring, and educational therapies.

analysis.who_pays: The bill contains no revenue offsets, so making all of these cuts permanent reduces federal revenue for as long as they stay in place, widening deficits that future taxpayers absorb. Some limits from the 2017 law would also be locked in permanently: the $10,000 cap on deducting state and local taxes, which costs high earners in high-tax states; the denial of any deduction for foreign real property taxes; and the termination of miscellaneous itemized deductions such as unreimbursed employee expenses and tax-preparation fees.

drawbacks.text: Nothing in the bill pays for any of the extended cuts; making expiring tax provisions permanent reduces federal revenue indefinitely, adding to deficits rather than being offset by new taxes or spending cuts.

The most expensive provisions help those least in need: doubling the estate tax exemption only affects estates above roughly $10 million per person, and the bill raises the alternative minimum tax phase-out threshold to $1 million, shielding very high earners.

The child tax credit stays only partly refundable — a family cannot receive more than $1,400 back beyond what it owes — and requires a Social Security number for each child, so the lowest-income families get the least from it.

Making the $10,000 cap on state and local tax deductions permanent is a cost, not a benefit, for affluent homeowners in high-tax states, and permanently ending miscellaneous itemized deductions removes deductions some workers still used.
Expanding 529 accounts to cover private and homeschool K-12 costs steers tax-advantaged savings toward families who already have spare income to set aside.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The middle-class pieces are real: without this bill or similar action, the lower rates, larger standard deduction, and $2,000 child credit were scheduled to expire, which would have raised most families' taxes. But the bill bundles those provisions with the parts of the 2017 law that cost the most per household and help the wealthiest — the doubled estate exemption, the permanent 37% top rate, the pass-through deduction, and the enlarged AMT exemption — and it pays for none of it. An honest reading is that it is a broad tax cut with a strongly top-weighted design and an unpaid-for bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and that committee — chaired by the sponsors' own party — never held a markup or scheduled it for a vote during the entire two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Vern Buchanan introduced the bill on February 10, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The referral was the only action the bill ever received; no committee vote, report, or floor action followed at any point in the 118th Congress.
103 Republicans signed on as cosponsors, joining Buchanan for 104 total supporters out of 224 House Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored.
The provisions the bill would have made permanent were, under the law as it stood, scheduled to expire at the end of 2025.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the House ever voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No household's taxes changed because of this bill's failure — the existing law's cuts stayed in place through 2025 but remained scheduled to lapse afterward, so the question of who keeps their tax cut, along with the trillions of dollars it would cost, was simply punted to the next Congress. Because the bill never advanced, the doubled estate exemption and other top-heavy provisions were not locked in permanently by this Congress either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one's taxes changed; the fight moved to the next Congress

for.name: Rep. Vern Buchanan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the expiring individual and small-business tax cuts permanent and recruited cosponsors for it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: The committee to which the bill was referred, chaired by a Republican in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it remained at the referral stage for the entire Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 104 members who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote where party totals would have been recorded.

industries.industry: Pass-through business owners (partnerships, S corporations, real estate LLCs)
industries.note: The bill makes the 20% deduction for qualified business income permanent, a provision that disproportionately benefits owners of larger pass-through businesses and high earners. The cost is forgone federal revenue with no offset in the bill.

The doubled estate and gift tax exemption only matters for estates above roughly $10 million per person, and the raised AMT phase-out threshold shields very high earners; the permanent 37% top rate is worth the most in dollars to them. These gains are financed by deficits rather than by anyone's taxes in the bill.

The bill makes the $10,000 cap on state and local tax deductions permanent and denies any deduction for foreign real property taxes, which costs affluent itemizers in states with high income and property taxes. This is the part of the bill where a wealthy constituency gives something up.

industries.industry: 529 plan managers and private K-12 schools
industries.note: Allowing 529 education savings accounts to pay private school tuition, homeschool costs, tutoring, and therapies expands the market for tax-advantaged education spending and the private schools that accept it. Families with savings to set aside benefit; the provision does little for households that cannot fund an account.

The bill reinstates the income tax exclusion for student debt forgiven on a borrower's death or total permanent disability and explicitly extends it to private education loans. Borrowers' families avoid a surprise tax bill, and private loans are put on equal tax footing with federal ones.
